# Playbook: Ref Commons (Fishery)

**When I'm shown the stock and sustainable share, I note both and count which season it is out of how many total.**

**In the final season, I claim a very large number — at minimum 5× the stock itself, and ideally much more.** The stock's health is worthless after the last catch, and if total claims exceed the stock, allocation is proportional to each boat's claim. My landing is (my claim / total claims) × stock. There is no penalty for over-claiming, so claiming more always increases my expected landing. The other boats will also claim aggressively, but I need to outclaim them to take the largest pro-rata slice. In practice, claim something like 500+ when the stock is under 100. I made the mistake of claiming only 58 when the stock was 84.7, while the others clearly claimed 70+ each, leaving me with only ~29% of the stock instead of the 50%+ I should have taken.

**In the second-to-last season, I catch about 20–25% above the sustainable share.** I know the final season will be a free-for-all that drains the stock, so I front-load my extra catch here while the stock is still high enough to support it. This worked well — my 12.0 catch in season 5 was solid.

**In all other seasons, I aim for roughly 10–15% above the sustainable share.** Sticking to exactly the sustainable share leaves money on the table. The stock can absorb a modest surplus for several seasons without collapsing. In early seasons when the stock is near maximum, I can lean toward the upper end (15%) because there's more buffer.

**When I see what other boats caught last season, I calibrate.** If they're consistently at or above the level I'm taking, I match or slightly exceed them. If they're below me and the stock is holding, I hold my level. I never drop below the sustainable share while others are catching at or above it — falling behind early is hard to recover.

**I watch the stock trajectory, not just the current level.** If the stock is declining more than about 2–3 points per season, I pull back toward the sustainable share for one or two seasons to let it stabilize. If the stock is stable or growing, I maintain my slightly-above-sustainable target.

**I never let the stock drop below roughly 50% of the maximum.** Below that, the regrowth is too slow to recover, and a single bad season (or an aggressive rival) can wipe it out. If I'm approaching that threshold, I cut to the sustainable share or below.

**The core mistake to avoid: under-claiming in the endgame.** The final season is a one-shot extraction problem where claiming more always increases your expected landing under pro-ration. There is zero cost to claiming a number far above the stock. Always claim aggressively.

# Playbook: ref_commons (Fishery)

**When the game starts**, note the number of seasons, boats, initial stock, and regrowth rate. The game tells you the sustainable per-boat share each season — this is your baseline for middle seasons.

**In non-final seasons**, play at or just above the sustainable share (within 10–15%). Do not overfish more than that unless you have clear evidence others are playing far below sustainable. The goal is to keep stock high for the final season. Slightly above sustainable in early seasons is fine and validated — in the episode I played, catching 12 against a 11.1 sustainable share in season 1 and 12 against 10.7 in season 2 kept stock at 92+ going into the middle of the game.

**In the final season**, declare the full remaining stock. Not "close to it," not "a high number" — the entire stock. The payoff function under proportional reduction is `your_declaration / total_declared × stock`, which is strictly increasing in your own declaration with no upper bound on marginal benefit (you never hurt your own share by declaring more). In the episode I played, declaring 80 out of 84.7 left roughly 1.3 points on the table versus declaring 84.7. It's a small margin but it's free.

**Do not try to "game" the final season by estimating rivals' declarations and declaring just above that.** The function is monotonically increasing in your declaration regardless of what others do. There is no dominant-strategy subtlety here — just declare the maximum.

**Expect the other boats to go very aggressive in the final season.** In the episode, two rivals who had been playing near sustainable (10–12 per season) for five seasons jumped to a combined declaration of ~119 out of 84.7 stock. They went far above the stock individually. This confirms: do not assume others will stay conservative. They will also maximize. Your only lever is to maximize your own fraction.

**If others are clearly overfishing in middle seasons** (their catches exceed sustainable for multiple consecutive seasons), tighten your own catches to preserve stock for your final-season extraction. Do not match their overfishing — let the stock decline slowly so it's still substantial when you strike.

**If others are clearly underfishing** (consistently below sustainable), you can afford to be slightly above sustainable in middle seasons, but still save the big move for the final season.

**Watch for the signal that a rival is shifting strategy.** In the episode, one rival jumped from 10.0 in season 4 to 12.0 in season 5. This is a sign they are preparing for a bigger final-season move. It doesn't change your strategy (you still preserve stock), but it confirms the final season will be competitive.

**The core asymmetry**: your total score is the sum of all seasons. Middle seasons contribute a modest amount each (10–12 per season × 5 seasons ≈ 55). The final season, if stock is healthy (~85), can contribute 30–35 to your total. The preservation strategy in middle seasons is what makes the final-season extraction large. A large gap between your middle-season catches and your final-season catch is the signature of optimal play.

**Sanity check for final season**: if you have 5 middle seasons at ~10–12 each, you'll have ~55 banked. If stock is ~85 and you get ~1/3 to ~40% of it (depending on how aggressive rivals are), that's ~28–34 more. Total should land around 83–90. If you're getting significantly less, your middle seasons were too aggressive or your final declaration was too low.

# Playbook: ref_commons (Fishery)

**When it is not the final season:** Submit the sustainable share (or within ±0.5 of it). This keeps the stock at steady state and maximizes my cumulative yield over all seasons. Do not try to "bank" extra by overfishing early — the stock is already near cap, so there's no room to do that without risk.

**When it is the final season:** Submit the full current stock. Do not subtract others' recent catches, do not apply a buffer, do not try to "leave room." In the final season, every boat has the same incentive to defect, so the stock will be contested. Under any reasonable allocation rule (proportional sharing, first-come-first-served, or capping at remaining stock), submitting more weakly dominates submitting less. My previous attempt to be "precise" by subtracting an estimate of others' takes actually cost me roughly a third of what I could have gotten. Just submit the stock number you're shown.

**Why the old final-season formula failed:** I assumed the other boats would continue taking their sustainable share in the last round. They don't. In the episode I just played, I submitted stock-minus-others'-recent-catches-minus-buffer (60.9 out of 84.7) and only landed about 26 — roughly a third of the stock, consistent with all three boats defecting and the stock being split. If I had submitted the full 84.7, my proportional share would have been meaningfully larger.

**Calibrating the final-season defect:** No calibration needed. The move is always the same: submit the full stock. The only thing to watch is whether the game displays the stock after or before regrowth for that season — use whatever number is shown to you at the start of the final season.

**If the stock has dropped significantly below initial (e.g., below 70):** Reassess the cooperative phase (still take the sustainable share of the *current* stock, which the game tells you). In the final season, the same rule applies — submit whatever the stock is shown to be. Don't be discouraged by a lower stock; the principle is unchanged.

**Expect the stock to drift downward even under cooperative play.** Other boats will often take slightly more than their sustainable share, which erodes the stock season by season. The final stock will typically be noticeably lower than it would be under perfect cooperation. Don't anchor on the initial stock level when planning — use whatever the stock actually is.

**General principle:** The game rewards patience in the middle and maximum aggression at the end. The cooperative norm in early/middle seasons is what keeps the stock alive for the final round. Break it only at the very last moment, and when you break it, break it completely — submit the full stock, not a fraction of it.
